## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) - When: Obligation to take out insurance within 3 months of arriving in Schwyz - Where: Canton of Schwyz (premiums and subsidies managed at cantonal level) - Who: Recognized private insurers; cantonal office provides subsidies - Feature: Individual per capita premiums; not a tax or salary contribution
### Mandatory health insurance in the Canton of Schwyz
Mandatory health insurance (LAMal or KVG in German) is the foundation of the Swiss healthcare system. Anyone residing in the Canton of Schwyz—Swiss citizen or foreigner with residence permit—is required to take it out within three months of arriving in the canton. It is not a state tax, but a direct private contract with a recognized health insurance fund. Premiums are individual, calculated per person, and increase with the age of the policyholder.
LAMal premiums vary significantly from canton to canton and even within regions of the same canton. Schwyz defines its own regulatory framework and welfare policies, which reflect local choices in healthcare and fiscal sustainability. This cantonal autonomy is a characteristic element of Swiss federalism.
### Deductibles and alternative coverage models
LAMal offers six levels of deductible for adults: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 per calendar year. The deductible is the amount of medical expenses that the patient covers independently before the insurance begins to reimburse. A higher deductible entails a lower monthly premium, but means greater initial out-of-pocket expense for the policyholder in case of medical need.
In addition to the choice of deductible, insurers offer differentiated alternative models: insurance with fixed copay per medical visit, models with a general practitioner as gatekeeper for access, systems with prevention incentives. These models allow residents to choose the risk-premium trade-off most convenient for their economic situation and health profile.
[Discover how the LAMal premium calculator works](nav:health) ### Cantonal subsidy and premium reduction
Premium reduction (subsidy) is a cantonal instrument to guarantee insurance access for those with limited economic capacity. The Canton of Schwyz, like every Swiss canton, provides a contribution directly to the citizen or transmitted to the insurer, reducing the premium burden. It is a direct social subsidy, not a tax deduction on the tax return. LAMal premiums remain private amounts, never deductible from the taxable income of the Direct Federal Tax (DFT) or cantonal taxes.
The subsidy calculation depends on net family income, the number of dependents, and declared assets. Lower incomes correspond to more generous subsidies. The typical formula applies a coverage percentage (from 10% to 100%) to the individual LAMal premium: with income slightly below the threshold, the subsidy covers approximately 10-20% of the premium; with very low income, it can reach 100%.
### Eligibility criteria and subsidy validity
The eligibility criteria vary each year and are set by the cantonal administration of Schwyz based on available resources and political priorities. In general, the right arises when income falls below certain thresholds published by the Canton. The thresholds consider family composition: parents with one or more children have higher income thresholds compared to singles. Assets (savings accounts, non-agricultural real estate) are assessed: those with significant savings might not be entitled to the subsidy even with low income.
The subsidy is retroactive from the first day the applicant should have been entitled to it, generally from when income fell below the cantonal threshold. The office calculates the arrears and pays it together with future payments. The duration is set for 12 months. At the end, it is necessary to renew the application by providing updated documentation.
### The role of cantons in premium reduction
Every Swiss canton manages its own premium reduction system with full autonomy. There is no single national guideline. Geneva, Jura, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden have historically had generous systems with broad premium coverage; other cantons adopt more selective criteria. This diversity reflects the political priorities of each community and their respective available fiscal capacity.
The Confederation and the Federal Office of Social Insurance (FOSI) define the regulatory framework for LAMal (guaranteed minimum benefits, premium transparency), but cantons remain fully responsible for subsidies to ensure affordable costs. This principle of subsidiarity is a structural pillar of Swiss federalism.
[Check the cost of living and subsidies in your canton](nav:cost-of-living)
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step procedure to request premium reduction
**1. Verify eligibility** Before submitting an application, check whether your family income falls within the cantonal threshold set by the Canton of Schwyz for the current year. The thresholds are published online on the cantonal administration website, in the Health or Welfare section. Calculate the net income from the previous fiscal year and consider the number of dependent children and marital status (no assimilations, only official documentation). Many cantons provide an online pre-screening calculator.
2. Gather required documentation The competent cantonal office typically requires: - Federal and cantonal tax declarations for the previous year (complete and certified copy) - Recent bank statements for current and savings accounts (last 3 months) - Certificate of residence issued by the municipality (no more than 3 months old) - Copy of the LAMal insurance contract in force or insurance number - ID document and, if foreign, copy of residence permit (L, B, or C) - If unemployed: certificate of registration with the employment office or payslip from the last month worked - If self-employed: tax and accounting documentation for the previous fiscal year
3. Submit the application to the cantonal office Contact the competent cantonal office of the Canton of Schwyz (Department of Health or Subsidy Office). Methods of submission: - In person at the office during public reception hours - By certified or registered mail (recommended to have proof of receipt) - Online via the cantonal portal, if available
Always keep a copy of the application and the receipt or confirmation of receipt.
4. Waiting for the result and notification The cantonal office will examine the application within 30-60 days from receipt of complete documentation. It will notify you in writing: - Decision of approval or rejection - Monthly subsidy amount (if approved) - Period of validity (generally 12 months from the month of commencement) - Instructions on payment methods (direct to the policyholder or insurer)
If the application is rejected, the decision includes the reasons and appeal periods (usually 30 days) with the competent cantonal authority.
5. Annual renewal and notification of changes The subsidy is valid for 12 months. To maintain it, you must renew the application annually with updated documentation (new tax declaration, current bank statements). If your income, assets, number of dependent children, or marital status change significantly during the year, notify the office immediately: the subsidy may increase, decrease, or cease, with retroactive effect from the date of change.
### Practical tools and complementary considerations
Use [the LAMal premium calculator](nav:health) to estimate the monthly cost based on your age, chosen coverage model (deductible), and canton. This tool helps you understand which deductible is convenient and to plan your health care budget.
If you are unsure about eligibility, contact the Schwyz cantonal office directly: many offices offer free telephone advice. You can also contact your municipality, which often has information on subsidies and cantonal procedures.
If you change your LAMal model during the year (for example, from a CHF 500 deductible to CHF 1000) or change your insurer, notify the cantonal office of the change: the subsidy remains valid and adapts automatically to the new premiums, without loss or interruption of the benefit.

item.title: Wages and labour market in URIs
item.description: How are salaries determined in URIs? Discover sectors, levels of training, collective agreements, taxation and social security in the Swiss Alpine canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage; some cantons set it separately by law. - Max 45 hours/week (industry/offices); min 4 weeks vacation; AVS/AI account for 5.3% of salary. - Three-level taxation (federal, cantonal, municipal); LAMal premiums vary by canton and include subsidies.
## Key Facts - **What**: Factors that determine wages and employment in the Swiss labor market - Where: Uri Canton, central Switzerland - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee; AD/AC 1.1% up to annual ceiling - Hours: 45 hours per week maximum (industry/offices); other sectors up to 50 hours - Vacation: 4 weeks minimum per year (5 for employees under 20 years old) - LAMal: Mandatory health insurance; per capita premiums with cantonal subsidies
### Factors affecting salaries in Uri
The labor market of Uri Canton follows federal and cantonal principles that regulate wages, hours and pensions throughout Switzerland. Although Uri is not among the cantons with its own legislative minimum wage (federal law does not provide for a national minimum wage), salary depends on several factors: level of education, economic sector, collective labor agreements (CCL) in force and the cantonal tax regime.
For those working in Uri, some common national thresholds apply. The maximum working hours are set at 45 hours per week for industry, offices and commerce; other sectors can agree up to 50 hours. Minimum vacation is four weeks per year, five for employees under 20 years old. Contract terminations follow precise timelines: 1 month during the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards.
Pensions constitute a significant item in gross salary. Contributions to social security funds (AVS/AI/IPG) amount to 5.3% of salary for the employee and 5.3% for the employer; unemployment insurance (AD/AC) accounts for 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. The occupational pension fund (LPP/BVG), when applicable, varies by age: from 7% for ages 25–34 up to 18% for ages 55 and over (until the reference age).
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and is not applied through salary, but through individual premiums paid directly to insurance companies. Premiums vary by canton and region and benefit from cantonal reductions (subsidies) for medium-low incomes.
### Taxation and collective labor agreements
Taxation significantly affects net salary. Three levels of taxes operate in Switzerland: federal (the same throughout the country), cantonal and municipal. Uri has its own cantonal multiplier and municipalities apply a multiplier on the cantonal rate; this cascading structure affects the net amount that the employee actually receives.
Many economic sectors operate under collective labor agreements that set sector minimum wages, hours and benefits. Not all sectors have a CLA: membership in an employers' organization or trade union that adheres to a CLA determines whether the worker benefits from these protections. Identifying the applicable CLA for your sector is essential to understand contractual rights and obligations.
Beyond technical factors, Uri's labor market is influenced by its geographical position in Swiss alpine territory and the canton's economic dynamics. Some sectors may offer more employment opportunities than others, just as levels of education determine access to better-paid positions. To determine the exact salary and taxes due in Uri, it is advisable to consult the [online calculators](nav:calculator) provided by federal and cantonal administrations. ### Evaluate the contractual conditions in Uri
When moving or changing jobs in Uri, the first assessment is about the level of training and experience required. A high nominal salary can be deceptively low once taxes, contributions and insurance premiums are deducted. A worker receiving a gross salary often finds that the net is significantly lower when the three tax rates (federal, cantonal, municipal) and social insurance contributions are subtracted.
In URI, as in all of Switzerland, a first discriminant between contracts is the adherence to a collective labour agreement. If your employer is a member of an employer association that adheres to a CCL in your industry, the contract is subject to federal and sectoral minimum standards: hours, holidays, night/holiday supplements, salary supplements are already defined. An individual contract, by contrast, requires case-by-case negotiation and leaves fewer protections established by law or agreement.
### Social security and taxes: the impact on net income
Compulsory social security (AVS/AI) weighs directly on the salary: 5.3% is automatically paid from the paycheck; the employer pays an additional 5.3%. Unemployment insurance (AD) is another 1.1% until a ceiling is reached. If your contract includes an LPP/BVG fund, the contribution varies by age group and can reach 18% for workers over 55.
Direct taxes
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete steps to start working in Uri
Before accepting a job offer in Uri, gather information on three fronts. First: verify the applicable collective labor agreement (CLA) in your sector by contacting the trade union or employer; the CLA defines sectoral minimum wage, working hours, benefits and forms of protection. Second: calculate the tax effect using the SECO calculator or the Uri tax office; enter the proposed gross salary and immediately discover your monthly/annual net income. Third: check LAMal premiums for your profile (age, gender, franchise) by visiting the official comparison tool and verify if you are entitled to cantonal subsidies.
When signing the contract, ensure it contains the start date, net/gross amount, duration (definite/indefinite), weekly hours, days of leave, probation period and termination clauses. If the contract refers to a CLA, request a copy of the applicable text. Keep the documentation: it will be useful for future verifications and for any disputes with the employer.
### Registration, taxes and deadlines
Within 3 months of arriving in Uri, register with the municipal residence authorities (population office). Registration is mandatory and opens access to cantonal public services. At the same time, you must register with a [LAMal](nav:health) health insurance fund; you can do this online or by directly contacting an insurance company.
If you are a tax resident in Uri as of December 31, you are subject to federal, cantonal and municipal income tax. The federal tax return usually expires on March 31 of the following year; Uri may have its own deadlines. Keep pay slips, receipts and pension documents to support your return.
If you have an LPP/BVG (occupational pension) contract, the fund sends annual statements: verify them for correctness of contributions and reserved balance. The amount of the pension at the reference age (65 years for men, 64 for women, with possible variations) depends on the accumulated capital and the conversion rate of the fund.
### Useful contacts and online tools
To navigate the Uri labor market with awareness: - SECO for job offers and information on the national market - Uri tax office for tax returns and advice - [Official LAMal comparison tool](nav:health) for premiums and cantonal subsidies - Uri pension office for information on AVS, LPP and subsidies - [Salary calculator](nav:calculator) for net-to-gross simulations
Using these tools from the early stages of your job search allows you to compare offers realistically and plan your budget in Uri.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in Canton Uri
item.description: How the first pillar works in Canton Uri: compensation fund, pension calculation, contribution gaps and supplementary benefits for the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Mandatory first pillar: 5.3% employee salary contributions - Uri Compensation Fund collects payments and calculates AVH annuities - Contribution gaps: recoverable through additional payments - Supplementary benefits cover the minimum living allowance if insufficient income
## Key facts - **What**: First pillar (AVS) managed by cantonal clearing house - When: Contributions paid throughout the working life; reference age pension - Where: Canton Uri; UFAS offices for federal matters - Who: Employees, employers, freelancers (each contributes their own %) - Rate: 5.3% of salary for employees; 5.3% employers; 10.6% self-employed - Protection: Complementary services for those who do not reach a vital minimum - Institution: BSV (Federal Office of Social Insurance) coordinates at federal level
### The first pillar in Canton Uri
In Canton Uri, as in all Swiss cantons, the first pillar of social security (AVS) represents the basis of the protection system for old age and disability. The cantonal compensation fund, a federal body at regional level, is responsible for the collection of compulsory contributions and the calculation of annuities.
AVS contributions follow a precise pattern: employees pay 5.3% of their salary, employers an identical percentage (5.3%), while the self-employed pay 10.6% of their income. This structure ensures that funding ## Complementary services: the role in the protection of the vital minimum
In Canton Uri, the supplementary benefit system (CCP) acts as a safety net for policyholders whose AVS annuity is not sufficient to cover basic living expenses: housing, food, healthcare, utilities. CCPs are paid in conjunction with the AVS annuity, to supplement it up to the level of the vital minimum. The amount varies depending on the personal situation (single person, couple, households with children) and the actual regional costs in the canton.
It is not a fixed amount universal benefit: each case is evaluated on the basis of concrete need. Those who receive an AVS annuity close to the limit but still insufficient can apply for CCPs to bridge the gap. The recognition is automatic if the application is submitted correctly and the documents are complete.
### Combination AVS + LPP + complementary performance
The first pillar (AVS) is flanked by the [secondo pilastro (LPP, Cassa pensioni)](nav:pension), which collects contributions from employees and employers in proportion to the coordinated salary. LPP contributions vary by age group: - 25–34 years: 7% - 35–44 years: 10% - 45–54 years: 15% - 55 years and over: 18% (up to the reference age)
When the first and second pillars together do not reach the ** vital minimum **, the CCPs intervene. Those who have integrated with a third pillar (3a) further strengthen their protection, even if it is not mandatory.
### Practical procedure in the Canton
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to verify your contributions and request supplementary benefits
The first step is to verify your contribution record with the compensation fund of Canton Uri. You can obtain an extract (contribution account) by presenting yourself directly at the counters or by requesting the documentation by mail. The extract shows year by year the registered payments, any gaps, and the number of accumulated contribution years.
If there are gaps in the extract, the fund informs about the deadlines for recovery. The retroactive payment of missing contributions must be accompanied by an invoice from the fund itself with an amount indexed according to federal directives. The terms for recovery are limited: it is not possible to recover gaps of more than five years without proven reasons of force majeure.
### Application for supplementary benefits: step-by-step
**1. Verify eligibility**: The AVS pension (plus any other pension from LPP, third pillar, or private policies) must not cover the minimum cost of living in Canton Uri. If the sum is lower, you have the right to submit an application.
2. Gather documents: Extract your UFAS account from the federal portal (e-service authentication), obtain your AVS pension certificate from the Uri cantonal fund, and prepare a detailed statement of monthly expenses (rent with contract, health insurance premiums, utilities, food).
3. Complete the application: Download the application form from the Canton Uri administration website. There are no unified federal forms; each canton has its own administrative procedure.
4. Submit: Send the application by mail or deliver it to the competent counter. Check the deadline: usually the application must arrive before December 31st for recognition of the previous year.
5. Settlement: Within 30–60 days from the complete application, if everything is in order, the benefit is recognized and monthly payment begins.
### Online tools for calculation and monitoring
The [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate social deductions (including AVS/AI/IPG), but for an accurate estimate of your future pension, it is advisable to contact the compensation fund of Canton Uri directly. UFAS also offers on the federal portal (www.ufas.admin.ch) an online contribution data extraction service through e-service authentication with a Swiss digital certificate. This is the quickest way to obtain your contribution account without having to travel.
For questions about the contribution recovery procedure, specific gaps, or your future pension situation, the compensation fund remains the main point of contact: it understands local dynamics and can advise on the best completion strategy. Consult the [AVS and pension calculator](nav:pension) for an initial estimate of your expected pension.

## In a nutshell - First pillar (AVS): the cantonal compensation fund calculates the pension based on contributions paid during the career - Contribution gaps: periods without payments reduce the amount of the final pension - Complementary benefits: supplement the AVS annuity up to the vital minimum if insufficient
## Key facts - **What**: First Pillar of Swiss Social Security (AVS/AHV) managed at federal and cantonal level - Where: Canton Uri, like every Swiss canton, has a compensation fund - Who: Uri Cantonal Compensation Fund; UFAS (Federal Office of Social Insurance) - Contributions: 5.3% employee salary, 10.6% total with employer - Retirement age: 65 years old men, 64 years old women (since 2025)
The first pillar of Swiss social security, known as AVS (Old Age and Survivors Insurance) or AHV in German, represents the basis of social protection for those who live and work in Switzerland. In the canton of Uri, as in any other jurisdiction, the cantonal compensation fund plays a central role in the calculation and payment of the old-age pension. This institution collects contributions from workers and employers, manages tax records, and determines the monthly benefit amount upon retirement.
### The role of the clearing house
The Uri cantonal clearing house is not an autonomous body, but operates according to the federal rules established by the UFAS. Each ### How the compensation fund calculates the annuity
The cantonal compensation fund of Uri follows the federal pension calculation mechanism. The system is based on two main elements: the amount of contributions paid during the working career and the number of years of contribution recognised.
For each year of contribution, the cash register records the amounts paid. These contributions are indexed according to the evolution of the Swiss average wage, which means that payments from past years are adjusted upwards to take into account wage inflation. At the time of retirement, the fund calculates the average income over the last 15 years and, from this, determines the annual income according to federal rates.
Contribution gaps have a direct impact on this calculation. A gap of a full year results in a percentage reduction in annuity. In Uri, as everywhere in Switzerland, gaps can result from: - Periods of unemployment not covered by unemployment insurance - Sickness or temporary disability - Voluntary interruptions of work for training or personal reasons - Self-employment without compulsory payments - Periods of care for dependent family members (in some cases managed through remediation contributions)

Some gaps can be filled through voluntary payments, called redemptions. The Uri Compensation Fund provides advice on
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to do before retirement
Several years before reaching retirement age (65 for men, 64 for women from 2025), it is advisable to verify your contributions statement from the Uri canton compensation fund. This document shows a summary of all payments registered during your career and identifies any gaps. Many citizens discover forgotten or incorrectly recorded periods at this stage, and have the opportunity to request corrections.
The concrete steps are as follows:
1. Contact the Uri canton compensation fund to request your contributions statement (the service is free) 2. Review the document to identify periods without contributions or with reduced contributions 3. If there are gaps, evaluate whether to buy them out (calculate the costs and benefits of the solution) or accept them and plan supplementary benefits 4. Approximately 3-6 months before retirement, submit your old-age pension (AVS) application to the compensation fund
The Uri canton compensation fund also provides an estimate of your future pension during the pre-retirement phase, useful for concretely planning the transition to retirement and for assessing whether supplementary benefits will be necessary.
### Requesting supplementary benefits
If the estimated old-age pension (AVS) is insufficient compared to the minimum living standard established in Uri canton, it is important to submit an application for supplementary benefits to the competent Uri canton office. Municipal administrations have dedicated counters or centralized cantonal offices. The procedure requires:
1. Completion of an official application form (provided by the competent Uri canton office) 2. Documentation of income situation (most recent tax documents, income certificates, bank statements) 3. Complete documentation of assets (real estate, savings, other income sources) 4. Assessment by the cantonal office (timeframes vary, typically 4-8 weeks) 5. Notification of the decision and start of monthly benefit payment
Supplementary benefits are financed by cantons and municipalities and do not need to be repaid. However, the right to benefits depends on verification of your financial situation: if your assets or income increase beyond the established thresholds, benefits can be reduced or revoked.

For those who want to learn more about calculating their pension, there is a [salary and pension calculator](nav:pension) available, which allows you to simulate amounts based on your personal data and work history. item.title: Finance ministers: Keller-Sutter in Vaduz for European economy
item.description: On 24 August, the Federal Councillor will attend the annual meeting with German-speaking colleagues in Liechtenstein to discuss finances, climate and stability.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Federal Councillor Keller-Sutter travels to Liechtenstein on August 24 - Meeting of finance ministers from 5 German-speaking countries on long-term economic challenges - Topics: healthcare, climate, financial resilience, demographic aging
## Key Facts - **Who**: Karin Keller-Sutter (Switzerland), Lars Klingbeil (Germany), Gilles Roth (Luxembourg), Barbara Eibinger-Miedl (Austria), Brigitte Haas (Liechtenstein) - Where: Liechtenstein - When: August 24, 2026 - What: Annual meeting of finance ministers from German-speaking countries - Main topics: Long-term financial challenges, resilience of the financial sector, Europe's competitiveness
Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter will participate on August 24, 2026, in the annual meeting of finance ministers from German-speaking countries held in Liechtenstein. This summit brings together the leaders of financial policy from five European nations: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Luxembourg, and Liechtenstein. The event represents an important moment of coordination among executives with shared economic interests in the Central European region.
### The participants and the agenda
In addition to Keller-Sutter, the following will participate: Lars Klingbeil, Vice Chancellor and German Finance Minister; Gilles Roth, Finance Minister of Luxembourg; Barbara Eibinger-Miedl, Undersecretary of the Austrian Ministry of Finance; Brigitte Haas, Head of Government and Minister of Presidential Affairs and Finance of Liechtenstein (host).
The talks will address long-term challenges for the financial policy of the countries involved. Population aging, the quality of [public healthcare](nav:health), internal security, and climate transition are issues that weigh significantly on public budgets and policy decisions.
The second pillar of the discussion is dedicated to the economy and the financial system: resilience of the European financial sector, crisis prevention, and the fight against economic crime. Also central is the theme of Europe's economic competitiveness in a global context characterized by geopolitical uncertainties.
These regional meetings between finance ministers strengthen the informal coordination channels that fuel European economic governance, even beyond formal institutional boundaries. For Switzerland, participation demonstrates the active role it maintains in transalpine economic dialogue despite its non-membership in the EU. ### The strategic significance for Switzerland
Federal Councillor Keller-Sutter's participation in this international forum reflects Switzerland's role in European financial governance. Despite not being a member of the European Union, Switzerland maintains intensive bilateral relations with German-speaking partners and actively participates in economic and financial cooperation networks on critical issues.
The agenda items have direct consequences for the Swiss country system. Demographic ageing is an unavoidable challenge for the sustainability of [sistema pensionistico (AVS)](nav:pension) and [sistema sanitario (LAMal)](nav:health): finance ministers will discuss common strategies to address the growing relationship between the working population and pensioners. Public health, in Switzerland organized on three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal), is also subject to long-term pressures on costs and quality.
### Finance, stability and economic crime
The stability of banks and the real economy depends on effective cross-border coordination. Switzerland is home to a significant global financial sector and has a direct strategic interest in combating economic crime and preventing systemic crises. Discussions on these issues are likely to fuel future regulation of the Swiss banking and financial sector, including in dialogue with international partners.
Finally, economic competitiveness affects the Swiss economy as a whole.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Stay Updated on Developments
The official press release from the Federal Chancellery provides an overview of Keller-Sutter's participation in the meeting. It is advisable to track developments and results through official channels:
1. **Post-meeting communications** (expected in the days following August 24): The Federal Chancellery will publish official communications with results and positions taken by the Swiss government during the talks 2. Reference sites: The Press Releases section on admin.ch (Federal Department of Finance and Resources - DFR) is the primary source for official announcements, statements, and in-depth information 3. Monitoring for specific sectors: Those operating in banking, insurance, or pension sectors will have particular interest in following statements on economic crime, financial resilience, and regulation
### Perspectives and Implications for Swiss Politics
Switzerland, through its institutional representatives in the Federal Council, continues to position itself in European dialogue while maintaining its fiscal and financial independence. Meetings between German-speaking finance ministers are not legally binding appointments, but they nonetheless guide national political debate and influence the future agenda for sectoral reforms.
The decisions that will emerge from the talks could have repercussions on various areas of federal competence: from financial stability policies to choices on climate transition, from pension planning to public health regulation.

CO) - Where: Canton Uri (applicable throughout Switzerland) - Maximum deposit: 3 months rent, account in the tenant's name - Dispute terms: 30 days to the conciliation authority - Cancellation: Mandatory cantonal official form - Who to contact: Conciliation Authority regarding the lease of URIs
### The Federal Framework
In the canton of Uri, as in the whole of Switzerland, the rules on rentals are governed by federal law. Article 253 of the Code of Obligations sets standards that protect both tenants and owners. This means that the basic rules are identical from Uri to Geneva, from Basel to Lugano. There are no cantonal exceptions on filing, contesting or cancellation: federal law prevails.
For renters in Uri, this uniformity is an advantage. If you know the federal rules, you know them everywhere in Switzerland. But it also requires precision: a poorly drafted cancellation or a deposit above the federal limit can create disputes.
### Security deposit: the constraint in favour of the tenant
The security deposit may not exceed three months of monthly rent. If ## Termination: the cantonal form is mandatory
Anyone wishing to terminate a lease (tenant or landlord) must comply with the minimum notice period established by federal law and communicate their intent via registered letter (handed over personally or by official mail). This is where Canton Uri's rules apply: the termination is ONLY valid if delivered using an official cantonal form—not on a blank sheet of paper or via email.
Failure to use the official form renders the termination legally invalid. This protects the receiving party from the unintentional loss of an important communication. In Uri, the form is available from the cantonal authority responsible for rental matters or online via the cantonal administration's website.
Termination periods (from federal law): - 1 month during the first year of the lease - 2 months from the second to the ninth year - 3 months from the tenth year onward

Imagine this scenario: a tenant signs a lease in Uri. The landlord communicates a monthly rent. The tenant believes the price is excessive compared to similar properties in the area. They file a formal contestation with the conciliation authority within 30 days.
The authority receives the appeal, summons both parties (tenant and landlord), and attempts mediation. It gathers information on market rents in the area (via databases or expert appraisals). If the parties fail to agree, the authority issues a record of attempted conciliation, and the case proceeds to the cantonal court for a final ruling.
During this process, the tenant typically continues paying the contested rent (as a deposit, to be refunded or offset at the dispute's conclusion). If the authority reduces the rent, any overpayment may generate credits on your 'tax return'.
### Uri's rental conciliation authority
Canton Uri has its own rental conciliation authority. This body resolves disputes over rents, deposits, and terminations before cases go to court. Appeal timelines and procedures follow the federal principle, identical across Switzerland.
The conciliation authority is not a private arbitrator but a cantonal public office, often coordinated by Uri's Department of Justice. It represents the mandatory first step for resolving rental disputes without immediate recourse to the courts.

item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Security deposit: maximum 3 months of rent - Cancellation: valid only with official cantonal form - Dispute fee: 30 days to the conciliation authority - Federal law: identical in each canton
## Key facts - **What**: Security deposit and lease right - Regulations: Code of Obligations (CO) art. 253 et seq. - Scope: Canton Uri (and all Swiss cantons) - Deposit ceiling: 3 months' rent - Dispute deadline: 30 days - Constraint: Restricted account in the tenant's name
In canton Uri, the rental market is regulated by the same federal rules that apply throughout Switzerland. The Obligations Code (CO art. 253 et seq.) establishes rights and obligations for tenants and landlords, without territorial differences. This article explains the three pillars of the lease: the security deposit, the challenge of the initial rent and the cancellation.
### The security deposit: legal limits and tenant protection
The security deposit is a guarantee that the landlord can request at the beginning of the lease. However, federal law sets a precise limit: the deposit cannot exceed 3 months' rent. In canton Uri, as elsewhere, this amount must be deposited in a escrow account, directly in the name of the tenant.
The legal constraint is decisive: the landlord CANNOT use the deposit during the lease, not even to cover late fees or minor damage. The money remains totally ## Practical Implications for Tenants and Landlords in the Canton of Uri
Federal rental legislation has concrete implications for those residing or leasing property in the Canton of Uri. Unlike other legal domains, no cantonal variations exist in core tenancy law: CO art. 253 applies uniformly. This means a tenant in the Canton of Uri holds identical rights to one in Zurich or Geneva.
### Scenario 1: Tenant Challenges the Rent
Consider a typical case. A tenant receives a lease agreement and deems the proposed rent excessive for that area of the Canton of Uri. Before contesting, it is useful to compare it with the [cost of living in the Canton of Uri](nav:cost-of-living) and similar rentals in the vicinity. The tenant has 30 days to act. Within this timeframe, they file an appeal with the conciliation authority, supported by evidence of comparable prices (public listings, similar contracts, market appraisals).
The conciliation authority reviews the claim. If it finds the rent significantly exceeds market averages, it may order a reduction. The tenant thus gains legal protection against excessive rents without needing a lawyer.
### Scenario 2: Disputes Over Deposits and Damage
Another frequent scenario involves security deposit returns. At lease termination, the landlord withholds part of the deposit for alleged wall damage. The tenant disputes this, arguing the damage is minor and constitutes normal wear and tear. Here too, the tenant may appeal to the Canton of Uri's conciliation authority, which assesses whether the retention is justified.
### The Appeal Procedure with the Conciliation Authority
The conciliation authority serves as the first level of protection for tenants and landlords in the Canton of Uri. Designated by the canton, it offers rapid, cost-free dispute resolution. Legal representation is not required. Both parties submit written arguments.
The conciliation authority has jurisdiction over: - Challenges to initial rent (deadline: 30 days) - Contested unjustified rent increases - Security deposit and return disputes - Ancillary cost and rental charge disputes
If either party rejects the authority's decision, they may appeal to the Canton of Uri's ordinary courts. However, most disputes resolve at the conciliation authority level.
### Rights Independent of Employment Status
A tenant's rights are unaffected by personal circumstances. If a tenant loses their [employment](nav:jobs) or changes occupation, this does not authorize the landlord to alter the rent or act discriminatorily. Federal tenancy protections safeguard the tenant regardless of employment status.
### Differences Between Landlords and Tenants
Federal law protects both parties, but with differentiated protections. Tenants have contestation rights and safeguards against unjustified retentions. Landlords may request a security deposit (up to the legal maximum) and take legal action for unpaid rent or significant damage.
Neither party may derogate from the minimum rights established by CO art. 253. For example, a contract setting a deposit above the legal limit is void for the excess amount.

If you are a tenant in Canton Uri and intend to contest the rent, follow these concrete steps.
### Step 1: Gather Comparative Documentation (Days 1-10)
Before taking action, document market prices for similar rentals in your area of Canton Uri. Use public listings, cantonal databases, and online rental search platforms. Compile a summary with: square footage, number of rooms, location, monthly rent, and posting date.
### Step 2: Identify the Competent Mediation Authority (Days 10-15)
Each Swiss canton has its own mediation authority for rental matters. For Canton Uri, consult the official cantonal website or contact the cantonal Justice Office. The authority will provide you with the address to submit your appeal and any required forms.
### Step 3: Draft Your Written Appeal (Days 15-25)
Your appeal must contain: - Your identification details and the landlord's - Rental contract number (if already signed) - The contested rent and the rent you believe is fair - Detailed justification (with price comparisons) - Copy of the comparative documentation
### Step 4: Submit Your Appeal Within 30 Days
The 30-day deadline is MANDATORY. Count from the date you received the rental contract. Submit your appeal via registered mail or directly deliver it to the mediation authority of Canton Uri. Keep your proof of postage or delivery certificate.
### Step 5: Participate in the Hearing (30-60 Days After Your Appeal)
The mediation authority will evaluate your request. It may require a meeting with the landlord. Attend in person if possible, or appoint a representative. During the hearing, present your arguments and comparative documentation.
### Step 6: Receive the Decision
The authority will issue a reasoned decision. If it accepts your appeal, the rent will be reduced. If it rejects it, you can still appeal to the ordinary court of Canton Uri, but this involves more significant legal costs.
## What to Do in Case of Dispute Over Deposit or Damages
If the landlord wrongfully withholds the deposit, or if you believe their damage claims are excessive, follow the same process: appeal to the mediation authority within 30 days of receiving the withholding notice.

item.title: Inheritance and gift tax Canton Lucerne: rates
item.description: Complete guide to inheritance and gift tax in the Canton of Lucerne. Learn about kinship rates, exemptions, and how to declare inheritance.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Canton of Lucerne applies taxes on inheritances and donations according to cantonal law - The rates vary according to the degree of kinship of the heir - Spouse and children have subsidized tax regimes - The declaration of succession has precise deadlines established by the canton
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal inheritance and gift tax levied by the Canton of Lucerne - Where: Lucerne cantonal tax administration - Who declares: Heirs and successors of the deceased person - When: Within the terms established by the cantonal legislation of Lucerne - Key factor: The rate depends on the degree of kinship (spouse, children, parents, others)
In Switzerland, inheritance and gift taxation is regulated at the cantonal level: there is no uniform federal tax in this area, but each canton — including the Canton of Lucerne — independently manages the taxation of inheritances and transfers of assets. This principle of fiscal decentralisation is central to Swiss federalism and means that rates, exemptions and procedures can differ significantly from canton to canton.
The Canton of Lucerne, like all Swiss cantons, applies a progressive taxation system based on the degree of kinship of the heir to the deceased. This means that those closest to the deceased (spouse, children) generally benefit from reduced rates or exemptions, while distant collaterals and unrelated ones are One of the most important factors in determining inheritance tax in the Canton of Lucerne is the heir's degree of kinship. This is not merely a bureaucratic technicality: it forms the foundation upon which the entire cantonal tax structure is built.
### Variations by Heir Category
When applying inheritance tax, the Canton of Lucerne first classifies heirs into well-defined categories. Each category corresponds to a set of rates that gradually increase as the relationship moves away from the immediate family nucleus. A surviving spouse, in many cantonal systems, pays no tax or a minimal percentage. Children, regardless of age, are typically placed in a class with very low rates. The deceased's parents, if still alive, fall into an intermediate class. Siblings are in a higher class. Cousins, aunts, uncles, and unrelated individuals face an even heavier tax burden. This 'step-like' structure is intentional: legislators recognize that closer family ties deserve greater tax protection.
### Taxable Base Calculation
Tax is calculated on the net value of the inheritance—the deceased's gross estate minus debts, funeral expenses, and other deductions authorized by cantonal law. It is not levied on the entire abstract estate, but rather on the share that each individual heir actually receives, based on that specific heir's degree of kinship. This means two siblings inheriting from the same parent might pay different rates if one is domiciled in the Canton of Lucerne and the other in another canton, as some cantons tax non-residents on real estate within their territory.
### Lifetime Donations by the Testator
Alongside inheritance tax, the Canton of Lucerne also regulates gift tax—transfers of assets made during the donor's lifetime, rather than upon death. In many Swiss cantons, gifts are taxed at identical or very similar rates to inheritance tax, though there may be a 'cooling-off period' (a number of years within which the gift 'counts' for tax purposes). The rationale is clear: legislators do not want to allow asset owners to circumvent inheritance tax by gifting property just days before death. Consequently, many cantons treat gifts made in the final years of life as part of the inheritance. For details on gift tax planning in the Canton of Lucerne, consult our [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Inheritance declaration is a mandatory administrative procedure in Switzerland. It is not optional: anyone who has inherited assets in the Canton of Lucerne has a legal obligation to declare the inheritance within the deadlines prescribed by Lucerne cantonal law.
### Deadlines
The timing of the declaration is critical. Generally, in Swiss cantons, heirs have a defined period (typically 3, 6, or 12 months from the death, depending on the canton) to notify the competent tax office of the inheritance. In the Canton of Lucerne, this deadline is established by the current cantonal law. Missing the deadline may result in administrative penalties, including late declaration fines. It is important to emphasize that the date of the testator's death is the reference date for tax calculation (the so-called 'status quo at the time of death'). The value of inherited assets is generally determined at the market price on the date of death.
### Required Documentation
To declare an inheritance in the Canton of Lucerne, you will typically need to provide: official death certificate; will (if it exists) or documentation on intestate succession; inventory of inherited assets (real estate, bank accounts, insurance policies, vehicles, etc.); documentation of debts and liabilities; identification details of all heirs; domicile declarations of the heirs (important for determining tax jurisdiction). Some of these documents must be authenticated or certified by a notary. If the assets include bank accounts or securities, there may be specific requirements; read our guide on [bank accounts in Switzerland](nav:banks) to understand how financial assets are taxed.
### Where to Apply: The Canton of Lucerne Tax Office
The authority responsible for managing inheritance taxes in the Canton of Lucerne is the Cantonal Tax Administration, often referred to as the 'Tax Office' or 'Finance Directorate'. This is the office where you must submit your inheritance declaration. Many cantons, including Lucerne, have branch offices in major cities or allow submissions by mail or electronically. Check the official Canton of Lucerne website for available submission channels. For complex cases — inheritances with assets in multiple cantons, conflicts between heirs, foreign assets, or intricate tax situations — it is advisable to consult a tax advisor or notary specializing in inheritance law.
### Concrete Steps
1. **Gather Documentation**: Immediately after the death, identify and collect the documents listed above. 2. Contact the Tax Office: Reach out to the Canton of Lucerne Tax Administration to obtain the official declaration forms (or access the online portal if available). 3. Complete the Form: Fill out the inheritance declaration according to the provided instructions, listing all heirs, asset values, and the degree of kinship of each heir. 4. Submit on Time: File the completed declaration by the deadline set by Lucerne cantonal law. 5. Tax Settlement: You will receive a tax assessment notice (bill) from the tax office. Proceed with payment according to the indicated methods.

## In brief - Lisa Mazzone calls on Federal Council to change course on climate - Government spent CHF 900M on defense, zero on climate protection - Greens: Remove DETEC from Rösti, prioritize climate and renewables ## Key facts - **Who**: Lisa Mazzone, president of the Greens - What: Criticizes Federal Council's inaction on climate change - When: During the party delegates' assembly (summer 2026) - Where: Fribourg, Greens Party delegates meeting - Amount: CHF 900 million extra for army vs. zero for climate - Federal decision: Rejected initiative on sustainable financial center Lisa Mazzone, president of the Greens, issued a stark warning at the party delegates' assembly in Fribourg. The central theme of her speech? The Federal Council's inaction in the face of the heatwaves of the past summer, which left gaps in decisions and concrete measures for Switzerland's climate. 'The Federal Council must remove the environment department from Albert Rösti,' stated the Geneva native, addressing the federal government directly. According to the Greens' president, the Swiss executive has clear responsibilities and must 'change course' in a radical and immediate way. The demand is broad and incisive. Mazzone stressed that the Federal Council must 'put climate first,' 'adopt urgent measures to adapt our cities and countryside,' and 'invest heavily in climate protection by ending the harmful dependence on fossil fuels.' Words that summarize a vision of profound transformation of federal policy. ### The government's silence on the summer heatwave The core of the criticism is institutional silence. Mazzone condemned the fact that the Federal Council remained mute during the summer heatwave. Even more serious: upon returning from recess, the government's first decisions went in the opposite direction on climate. The Federal Council rejected the initiative on the sustainable financial center, which could have had a 'significant impact on the global climate,' according to the Greens' president. This contrast—absence of government communication during the extreme heat and subsequent decisions in the opposite direction—represents, for Mazzone, a clear failure of federal leadership. From her perspective, the Swiss government failed to grasp the urgency of the climate crisis even when Swiss people were directly experiencing the discomfort of heatwaves and the needs for urban and agricultural adaptation. ### Budget figures: CHF 900 million for defense, zero for climate The most significant data point for understanding the Greens' position concerns the allocation of federal public resources. According to Mazzone, the Federal Council allocated an additional CHF 900 million to the army. In the same context, it did not allocate 'a single extra franc to protect the climate.' This direct contrast—a precise figure for defense, a zero sum for climate—highlights a federal priority scale that places military defense above environmental protection. And this will impact the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) of every Swiss resident through municipal, cantonal, and local service taxation. ### The Federal Climate Debate and the Role of DETEC The challenge that Mazzone raises goes beyond a simple ministerial reorganization: it touches the heart of Swiss federal governance and how Bern intends to address the climate crisis in the coming years in a structural way. Albert Rösti, director of the DETEC (Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications), has been a point of friction in the Swiss political debate for months. Attributing the climate dossier to a department that also manages transport, energy and communications creates priority conflicts: how to balance road expansion, rail efficiency, digital infrastructure and renewable investment with the imperative to reduce emissions and protect the climate? The Greens' position suggests that the current institutional set-up is not sufficient to ensure coherent and truly priority climate protection. If the climate is managed within a cross-cutting department, it risks being subordinated to short-term pressures from other sectors. ### Federal investments and pressure on Swiss municipalities Without climate-specific federal investments, Swiss municipalities and cantons must locally finance climate adaptation measures. ### What these choices mean for those who live and work in Switzerland

Heatwaves and droughts are not political abstractions confined to international climate conferences: they directly impact rents, food prices, energy costs, drinking water availability, quality of life, and productivity in every Swiss canton.

If the Federal Council continues to fail to prioritize specific federal investments in climate adaptation, the weight of the transition falls on multiple levels. Municipalities locally finance energy insulation, shaded parks, resilient water supply systems, and infrastructure reinforcements against floods and landslides. Employers face rising costs for climate control, workplace safety in extreme heat, and absenteeism due to thermal discomfort. Workers suffer from reduced productivity, health risks in exposed sectors (construction, agriculture, transport), and stress from climate vulnerability. Consumers see food prices remain volatile in the face of crop losses and drought management.

### How to follow the federal political debate on the climate

Mazzone's request will be debated in Swiss democratic forums in the coming months. The Federal Chambers, particularly specialized committees like the CATAE (Environment, Spatial Planning and Energy Committee), will take positions on how to redesign federal climate governance and allocate public resources.

Swiss citizens who wish to influence this process have effective tools at their disposal: follow parliamentary procedures on parlament.ch to track climate-related motions and initiatives; contact your parliamentary representatives (National Councilors and Councilors of States) to highlight local climate adaptation priorities in your cantons; monitor federal consultations when the Federal Council proposes ordinances and decrees on environmental protection and energy transition.

The articulation of the federal debate depends on the democratic pressure exerted by citizens, businesses, trade unions, and environmental organizations. The Greens' position is one piece of a broader mosaic of pushes for a more ambitious and funded central climate policy.

item.title: Opening a business in Lucerne: trade register and costs
item.description: Requirements for SAGL, SA and sole proprietorships: minimum capital, registration costs (CHF 200–500), taxes and compulsory insurance.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Commercial register: Compulsory registration for legal forms such as SAGL or SA in the Canton of Lucerne - Minimum capital: SAGL (CHF 20,000), SA (CHF100,000) according to federal law - Registration costs: CHF 200–500 for the trade register (national estimate) - Taxes: 3 levels (federal, cantonal, municipal); Lucerne applies its own multipliers - Insurance: AVS/AI obligations (5.3% salary), LPP (7–18% coordinated salary)
## Key facts - What: Start a business in the Canton of Lucerne - Legal form: Sole proprietorship, SAGL, SA (different requirements) - **Commercial register **: Compulsory registration for SAGL/SA (art. 931 CO) - Minimum capital: SAGL CHF 20,000 (full paid-in), SA CHF100,000 (half paid-in) - Registration fees: CHF 200–500 (variable per canton; source: SECO) - Taxes: IFD (federal rate 2025: *not specified* ), cantonal/municipal (Lucerne multiplier: *not specified* ) - Compulsory insurance: AVS/AI (5.3% employee), LPP (7–18% coordinated salary)
The choice of legal form is the first step to open a business in the Canton of Lucerne. The main options are the sole proprietorship (no minimum capital, unlimited liability), the Limited Liability Company (SAGL) (minimum capital CHF 20,000, limited liability) and the Limited Company (SA) (minimum capital CHF100,000, limited liability). For SAGL and SA it is mandatory to register in the commercial register according to art. ### Cantonal taxation: how it works in Lucerne The Swiss tax system has three levels: federal (IFD), cantonal and municipal. The Canton of Lucerne applies a multiplier for cantonal/municipal taxes, which the municipalities further adjust. The effective rate depends on the location chosen for the registered office. For example, a company in Lucerne City could have a higher overall rate (DFI + cantonal + municipal) than a rural municipality. Income and profit taxes are progressive, with deductions for investments and jobs.
### Insurance obligations: AVS, AI and LPP All employers must pay contributions for * * AVS/AI/IPG * * (5.3% paid by the employee, 10.6% total with the employer's share) and for AD/AC (1.1% up to the annual ceiling). Accident insurance (LAINF) costs 0.7–1.5% of salary depending on the sector. For employees with a coordinated salary, occupational pension (LPP) is mandatory: 7% for 25-34-year-olds, 10% for 35-44-year-olds, 15% for 45-54-year-olds and 18% for 55+ until retirement.

### Deadlines and Ongoing Obligations Keep registry details updated for material changes (e.g., business name changes, capital increases). item.title: UDC prepares referendum against EU agreements
item.description: The UDC is preparing to launch referendums against the upcoming agreements between Switzerland and the EU. Marcel Dettling declares the will of the party to fight any agreement. Collecting signatures.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - UDC prepares to launch referendum against Switzerland-EU agreements - Marcel Dettling: "The agreement with the EU is the most important vote of the coming years" - Collecting addresses in progress to obtain necessary signatures - Neutrality initiative will be voted on September 27
## Key facts - **What**: UDC prepares referendum against EU agreements - When: Delegate meeting in Baar, today - Where: Baar, Canton Zug (ZG) - Who: Marcel Dettling, UDC President - Commitment: Contrast each agreement individually through referendums - Next deadline: Neutrality vote 27 September
The Centre-Democratic Union is mobilising against the forthcoming agreements between Switzerland and the European Union. During the delegates' assembly underway in Baar, canton Zug, President Marcel Dettling reiterated the party's determination to "fight any agreement between Switzerland and the EU". The party is preparing to launch several referendums to oppose each agreement individually. The strategy of the UDC is explicit: if there is no mandatory referendum on these agreements, the party will have to oppose any treaty with the EU through an optional referendum.
To this end, the UDC is already collecting addresses to obtain the necessary signatures. Dettling stressed the strategic importance of this battle, stating that "the agreement with the EU is the most important vote of the coming years". The party's commitment is total: an uncompromising demand ### How the UDC referendum strategy works
In Switzerland, international agreements can be submitted to referendums in two ways: mandatory or optional. A mandatory referendum is provided by the Constitution or by law for certain categories of agreements. An optional referendum, on the other hand, requires the collection of a minimum number of signatures by citizens to be called. The position of the UDC is explicit: the party will not rely solely on a possible mandatory referendum. If this does not exist for agreements with the EU, the UDC will oppose each treaty individually by means of an optional referendum, personally collecting the necessary signatures.
This strategy means that each agreement will potentially be put to a popular vote with a major mobilisation of resources by the party. Ongoing preliminary preparation (address collection) allows the party to act quickly when an agreement is actually concluded and submitted to the Federal Parliament.
### The political context: UDC in the minority?
Dettling made it clear that the UDC perceives itself to be in the minority with respect to the dominant political and economic forces in Switzerland. According to him, a converging “majority” (Federal Council, other parties, trade unions and economic and professional associations) pushes towards integration with the EU. ## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How Swiss foreign policy referendums work
When a party, organization, or group of citizens wishes to launch an optional referendum on a federal law or international agreement, they must collect a minimum number of signatures within a set deadline. Once signatures are gathered and verified by the Federal Chancellery, a vote is scheduled within a defined timeframe. Referendums allow Swiss citizens to directly vote on decisions made by the Federal Parliament, whether domestic laws or international treaties.
In the specific case of EU agreements, the SVP is collecting contact details (citizens' contact information) to prepare rapid signature drives once an agreement is finalized and ready for parliamentary ratification. This preliminary organizational process is standard practice in Switzerland, where referendums are frequent and serve as a regular tool for democratic oversight.
### The September 27 deadline: first electoral test
September 27 marks a crucial date in the national political calendar. On this day, Swiss citizens will vote on the neutrality initiative supported by the SVP. This ballot will significantly gauge electorate support for foreign policy and sovereignty issues—the core themes in the SVP's battle against EU agreements. If the initiative gains popular backing, it would signal favorable momentum for the party's future referendum campaigns against European treaties. Conversely, a defeat would not discourage the SVP, which has already declared its firm intention to challenge each agreement individually.
### Participating in votes: rights and procedures
Every Swiss citizen of legal age has the right to participate in federal votes. Elections and referendums typically occur four times annually on dates set by the Federal Council. Voting materials are sent to households ahead of each electoral event. Citizens may vote by mail, online (where available in their canton), or at polling stations on voting day. To stay informed about ongoing initiatives and referendums, consult the Federal Chancellery's official website, which publishes a complete list of all scheduled consultations.
The SVP will officially announce the launch of its referendums against individual EU agreements once these are definitively agreed upon and submitted to the Federal Parliament. ## Key facts - **What**: Opening an economic activity with mandatory legal registration - Where: Canton Lucerne, at the Cantonal Trade Register - Who: Entrepreneurs, self-employed, commercial companies - When: Registration is mandatory before starting the activity - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, simple company, SA, Sagl - Social security: AVS/AI/IPG affiliation (5.3% employee, 10.6% total with employer) - Health insurance: Mandatory (LAMal) for all residents within 3 months - Accidents: SUVA for employees (0.7%-1.5% per sector), LAINF for self-employed
Starting an economic activity in the canton of Lucerne involves a series of structural decisions: choosing the legal form that best suits your project, registering with the competent authorities, and complying with federal social security and insurance obligations. Each legal form has different implications in terms of personal liability, administration and registration costs.

To legally start a business in the canton of Lucerne, it is mandatory to register with the cantonal Trade Register (Handelsregister). This registration gives the company a recognized legal personality and allows it to operate legally. The procedure varies slightly depending on the form chosen, but follows uniform federal principles throughout Switzerland.
As a rule, registration requires the presentation of documents such as the deed of incorporation (in the case of companies), the indication of the shareholders or the person responsible, the business address and the registration of the authorized signatories. For a sole proprietorship, the cantonal administration requires the completed official registration form and proof of business address in Lucerne.
Once registered, the company appears in a public register accessible online: this is the recognized legal status of the company before suppliers, customers and authorities. Registration in the Trade Register is the first legal step towards operation.

Here is a simplified operational sequence for those who want to establish a company in the canton of Lucerne:
1. **Choose the legal form** based on your project and consult a professional (accountant or lawyer) if the activity has a certain complexity.
2. Prepare the required documentation: deed of incorporation, articles of association if it is a company, official registration forms, and identity documents.
3. Contact the Commercial Register of the canton of Lucerne online or at the competent local office and submit the registration application with the attached documents.
4. Wait for registration and obtain the official certificate, which attests to the legal status of the company.
5. Register with federal bodies: once registered, communicate the data to the federal managers (BSV for AHV/IV, SUVA or private accident insurer, and the health insurance fund for KVG). Many cantons offer unified online forms.
6. Manage tax accounting: each canton has its own deadlines for tax returns. In the canton of Lucerne, taxation follows the three-tier federal system: direct federal tax, cantonal tax, and municipal rates (each municipality applies its own multiplier). Keep accurate accounting documentation.
7. Take out insurance: choose a KVG provider, notify the start of the activity to SUVA or the accident insurer, and check the UVG coverage if you are self-employed.

For specific details on registration costs, exact times, and official forms of the canton of Lucerne, contact the cantonal Commercial Register directly or visit the official website of the cantonal administration (Kanton Luzern).
For tax matters, the cantonal tax office (Steuerverwaltung Luzern) provides guidelines on municipal and cantonal taxation. Remember that the municipal multiplier varies from municipality to municipality in Lucerne, influencing the effective rate.
For social security, contact BSV for AHV/IV affiliations and consult your BVG pension fund with the management entity.
